newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-DU PLESSIS POSES MORE QUESTIONS THAN ANSWERS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-DU PLESSIS POSES MORE QUESTIONS THAN ANSWERS.

text.p: If the British Lions are uncertain what to expect from Carel du Plessis's Springboks in the forthcoming series, they can join the club.
South Africa's large rugby worshipping public is waiting with bated breath for the unveiling of the rugby vision of their country's new coach.
At the age of 36, du Plessis is not only South Africa's youngest rugby leader but also arguably the most mysterious.
Is he the Messiah or is he the Mistake -- an untried novice, out of his depth?

Since he ended a glittering playing career in 1989 with a fifth Currie Cup title for Western Province, du Plessis had not been involved in the playing, coaching or rugby administration in any significant way.

His return to the colours came only in November when he was plucked from the trading floor of the Cape Town corporate services company, where he was a partner, to become tactical adviser to predecessor Andre Markgraaff on the Springboks' all-conquering tour of Argentina, France and Wales.

When Markgraaff resigned in disgrace following the release of a tape containing racial slurs, du Plessis was not the popular favourite to succeed him. The job was expected to go to Springbok forwards coach Nick Mallett, who had also turned provincial minnows Boland into a respected outfit.

When the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) announced that Carel Johan du Plessis would be their fifth coach in as many years the appointment was greeted by the South African press as a gamble at best and a blunder at worst.

His coaching CV was almost blank, containing only a brief spell as assistant coach at the unfashionable University of the Western Cape club. His first act was to dispense with the services of Mallett and backs coach Hugh Reece-Edwards and appointhis former Western Province team mate, the taciturn Gert Smal, 35, as forwards' coach.
"When I made myself available I knew there would be questions raised about my suitability as it's traditionally a post filled by someone who has served their time as a coach," said du Plessis.
"There will be criticism, there might be a few positive remarks six months down the line but it really is the hot seat.
"We now have to produce the goods in the way we want to play the game and in the results. Those are the big motivational factors."
But how will he play the game? "Classical" and "traditional" are descriptions journalists have tried to pin on du Plessis's deliberately evasive talk of his rugby vision.

He has mildly criticised South Africa's style of last season as being "one-dimensional" but also said he will not vary much from the game plan which saw the Springboks end their season with a five try to one demolition of Wales in Cardiff.
"I don't want to say too much but it certainly involves backline play which I believe we can use to better effect," is almost as much as du Plessis will concede.
"There won't be major changes. Just enough to give the players one or two tactical options.

"We have a very good pack of talented forwards and backline players and I think we should allow their creativity to come out. I think there may have been players who were frustrated by the lack of a game plan that allowed them to try anything different."
Du Plessis learnt his rugby at Stellenbosch University under the late godfather of the South African game, Dr Danie Craven, before joining Western Province.
In the isolation-hit 1980s du Plessis played only 12 times for the Springboks -- alongside brothers Michael and Willie -- scoring four tries from the left wing.

He is regarded as his country's greatest ever in the position and was also a highly successful captain of Western Province scoring a remarkable 81 tries in 108 matches as the Province bestrode South African rugby during the decade.
He is married with two small children and the flashing temper he exhibited as a player has been conquered by his renewed faith.
"We have been a Christian family for the last few years and I trust in the Lord's guidance in my life," he said.
"I had a temper as a player and it doesn't disappear but I believe because of my spiritual beliefs, my Christian beliefs, I can overcome it."
Du Plessis's temper has yet to be tested in his new post. He is a modest and likeable young professional who does not naturally seek the limelight. Reserved? A classic nice guy?
"I wouldn't say I'm reserved -- that could be misinterpreted -- but I'm not interested in being flashy or singing from the rooftops," he said.
"I'm results driven and they will speak for me."

The 13 tests du Plessis faces in his first season begin with a Cape Town international against Tonga on June 10 but begin in earnest with the first of three tests against the British Lions -- also in Cape Town -- on June 21.
"I believe they will come and try and stamp their authority in the forward play. We will have to contain them up front -- that's where their strengths will be," said du Plessis.
"What makes them a dangerous side is that they are trying to bring something new into their game. They will attempt to be more attacking, more expansive, to try and really move the ball.
"If they find the right combinations they will be really tough opposition."
